Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Known People: Related people, Feeling Happy: Feeling happy or relaxed, Discomfort: Feeling uncomfortable
  Maladaptive Strategies: Stay Near Exit: make sure to stay close to exit, Overeat: eat excessively to manage distress, Heavy Makeup: heavy make-up
  Threat: Body on Alert: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger, Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard, Door and Lock Checking: I repeatedly check that doors and windows are locked
  Memory: Memory Replay: My memories of the frightening event are like a film that plays over and over., Vivid Memory: My memories of the frightening event are very clear and detailed., Uncontrolled Access: The memory forces its way into my mind when I do not want it to
  Negative Appraisals: Others-Would-Cope: Somebody else would have stopped the event from happening, No Longer Capable: I am no longer capable of doing the things that defined me, Defective Self: There is something wrong with me as a person

Vignette:
Two years ago, at a family reunion in rural Oregon, Mere Liou, a 56-year-old American of Polynesian heritage, found herself trapped in a guest house with her cousin. What began as an evening of shared meals and familiar jokes turned violent when he cornered her in the back bedroom. She remembers the exact grain of the wallpaper, the heavy smell of his cologne, the precise pitch of his voice, and the way the floorboards groaned under his weight. She froze, unable to break free, and when it ended, the house remained filled with the same relatives who had served the casseroles just hours before. The familiarity of his face, the collapse of what should have been safe ground, and the sudden violation of a space where laughter had just echoed are what make the return of old faces so potent. She had come to believe there was something fundamentally wrong with her as a person, that she should have been able to break free or shout for help, and she was certain someone else at that reunion should have seen what was happening and stepped in. Since that night, the memory does not fade. It plays in her mind like a film that will not stop, demanding she watch the same angle of shadow on the ceiling, the exact condensation on the window, the precise sequence of his movements. It forces its way into her thoughts during morning coffee, while folding laundry, or standing at the intake desk of the community social ministry she directs. Her body never quite believes the danger has passed. She wakes each morning already braced, her shoulders knotted and her breath shallow, as though she is waiting for a threat she cannot name. She walks through the ministry offices with her eyes constantly mapping the room, counting the windows, tracking who enters. She no longer feels capable of doing the things that defined her—sitting in the middle of a circle, holding a grieving mother’s hand without scanning for a way out, trusting the warmth of a room that might turn cold. Across the weeks and months that followed, parallel routines solidified. Each morning before her ministry rounds, Mere applies thick concealer, heavy contour, and a full set of lashes, her hands steady as she builds a barrier over her skin. When the memories spike or the room feels too tight, she retreats to the kitchen and eats larger portions than usual, meals that linger, snacks she does not need. She does not sit in the center of her office; she makes sure to stay close to the side exit, her purse already half-zipped. Her husband, David, has noticed the distance. He asks why she flinches when he touches her shoulder, why she cancels their anniversary dinner, why she now avoids the crowded fellowship hall where she once led evening outreach groups. What frightened her most was the realization that the moment she felt happy or relaxed, her body would suddenly register the same discomfort it had in that bedroom. When a teenage client at the ministry laughs loudly at a shared joke, Mere’s jaw tightens and she steps back, acutely aware of how far the door is from where she stands. She trades shared laughter for the safety of her own four walls, leaving the group meals unfinished. The weight of it all finally brought her to my office last month. She sat on the edge of the chair, her hands folded tightly in her lap, her makeup immaculate despite the hour. She told me she is exhausted from guarding a house that does not need guarding, from checking the deadbolt three times and testing the window latches until her thumbs ache, from flinching at the very people who have never hurt her. She wants to know if she will ever feel safe in her own skin again, and if the woman who used to lead those morning prayer groups can still exist somewhere beneath the armor she has built.
